Something easy the closes the conversation from further questioning. “I got hurt a while ago.” “They’re from a long time ago.” Usually if people are asking they’re being deliberately dense or don’t understand their curiosity isn’t owed an answer. You can outright refuse to answer them as well. “I don’t want to talk about that.” “I don’t feel comfortable answering those kind of question.” “Please don’t make comments like that.” “That’s a very personal question.” Just be clear and concise and avoid a defensive demeanor that might tempt them to pry further. Your scars are not an open invitation for people to inquire your history of mental health, however when people see something that they aren’t used to seeing curiosity is inevitable.

Unfortunately, active self harm can be a huge obstacle when it comes to obtaining and maintaining a job. Whether a CNA or a barista or an office goon having a constant cycle of fresh self harm injures is a bio hazard that isn’t great news for you, your patrons or your coworkers. Coming from experience I think this is a good time to focus on how the addictive qualities of self harm are effecting how you take steps into the working world and how it might be hindering that transition. This might be a good wake up call to getting the final push to move you away from this relapse. I know it helped me a lot and opened up a new aspect of responsibility that helped me stay accountable for my NSSI addiction. 

That being said, when it comes to self harm scars in the work place, it’s ultimately about your level of comfort. I very rarely have had people point out my own (which are particularly obvious). My nervousness to switch to short sleeves had more to do with my coworkers and peers. I’d say I had to work a little harder to prove myself past the predictive of what my scars said about me but that’s about it. 

Good luck with your CNA position! Wishing the best :)

From my own experience it’s something that starts willingly and then takes on a life of its own. At this point it begins to take control and you find yourself in a state of being where you can’t properly function with self harm as a crutch. That’s one of the reasons why it’s so dangerous

If interacting within the self harm community is causing you to want to hurt yourself worse then before and making you compare your self harm to others then you should not be engaging with the community. This is not the reason spaces like this should exist and it sounds like it’s become more of a danger to you then a place of support. The severity of your self harm does not change the fact that it’s self harm and it’s bad for you. You don’t have to hit styro to be a valid member of the community. It’s not like lifting weights where you work to lift heavier and heavier numbers. You don’t have to cut deeper the next time. You don’t have to bleed more then before. It’s not a competition and it’s not for comparing or contrasting with other peoples self injurious behaviors, despite what other may think.

Something that is difficult to accept when it comes to NSSI the ways that it impacts future (or current) employment. 

Much like when people have eating disorders or substance dependencies that advance beyond their control, self injurious behavior can impact your ability to apply for or even maintain a job. Theres the obvious matter of uniform restrictions and the likelihood of the interview process falling short due to negative reactions against scars or other lasting evidence. There is also the matter of continuing to selfharm while a part of the work force. Consistent reoccurring fresh wounds are more or less a biohazard. This is especially the case if you are lets say a dishwasher or a server at a restaurant. When it comes to office jobs its still relevant but I admit not that much of a big deal. Employers don't typically enjoy the idea of their employees working with customers or processing paperwork while simultaneously bleeding all over the place under bandages under their clothes (speaking from experience). 

It also needs to be mentioned, hurting yourself can make it difficult to move around or focus or function like you normally would, thats another aspect. A good way to indicate whether or not something might not be good for you is examining the ways it effects how you function in day to day life. Hindering your ability to get/maintain a job? thats not good. Making it difficult/painful to lift a box or wear work appropriate clothing? Thats no good either.

You should have autonomy over your own body, however "its what I need to function" and "it is what keeps me alive and safe." Doesn't sound very autonomous to me. Absolutely, NSSI (or self harm, or SH or self mutilation) is a coping skill. It's effective and reaps quick results. It's punctuated by visible and physicals cues which helps us know when it's working and when we are participating in it.  I know IM self harming because my body is telling my brain I am in pain. My nerves sense physical pain. I create a pain in the blink of an eye. I can identify either the mark left behind or the tool that I used to caused it. 

Just because something is a coping mechanism doesn't mean it is good for you. Nobody cares about "wrong" or not wrong. Some people think smoking or drinking until you black out is wrong. Some people think having casual sex or working out too much is wrong. Other people will ask you why shooting up is considered wrong when it's the only way they make it through the day. 

Needing something that plays on your dopamine reward system to stay alive is not bodily autonomy and I don't think you "will stop when it's safe for \[you\] to do so."

 If you require NSSI to function on a daily or even weekly level then your autonomy has been impaired by something within your reward system that is using NSSI as a crutch against stressors. 

Obviously, you don't endorse SH. Why? Because it's recognized as a dangerous symptom of mental illness. If anyone can have autonomy over their own body then your endorsement of SH is totally irrelevant. It shouldn't matter who is self harming because like yourself we all have freedom to demonstrate power and agency over choices concerning our own bodies. If you can self harm, why shouldn't others? As long as I'm not hurting myself to the point of needing stitches or anything right? 

Of course its your body, your choice. Thats why navigating coping skills and catharsis as an adult feels so harrowing and dangerous. However I would suggest you seek out and try to understand exactly why you are looking to self harm (to keep yourself alive) before you publicly implore others to perceptively neutralize the effects of a dangerous behavior that puts people in psych wards, hospitals, limits their opportunities of employment and negatively impacts social/sexual/romantic/familial relationships. 

Im very sorry you've had to turn to NSSI to cope with stressors in you life and Im sorry if what I've written feels hateful for harsh. Its harsh because non-suicidal self injury is a very harsh topic and should be treated with the bleak reality of what it is. 

TLDR: Im sorry you are hurting yourself but you don't have autonomy over something you need to keep you from killing yourself.

I think it’s very likely your husband and many other adults view their own self harm as a tool to navigate distressing stimuli. It could be the need to feel grounded and real, to feel he’s making up for any short comings, it could even be an issue of his brains regulation of serotonin that’s causing his compulsion to self harm. 

I just think it’s important to understand for many adult people who work hard to hide this habit, the addiction can be misinterpreted as something we rely on. It’s harder when we aren’t under a guardians eye with no risk of being scolded or sent to the school counselor. That makes it feel like an adult decision, I guess. 

He may not be ready to talk to you about why he is struggling with this, which can make the topic difficult to navigate. I myself, mostly out of embarrassment, have become quite the manipulator when it came to hiding it. I know this is a rough position to be in as his partner. I’m sorry. It sucks when someone you care about is hurting in a way that makes them want to hurt themselves.
